#10113. The Jensen Huang saga could be the beginning of the end of the AI bubble – or just a boon for competitors

There could be no greater irony than if the misdeeds of one of AI's biggest names brought the whole house of cards crashing down

KETTLE Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia after a trio of affairs that include an alleged Chinese spy and two of his subordinates, turning the week into one that's shaken the tech sector.

What will become of Nvidia now that its only leader in 33 years, and one whose vision shaped the company into one of the largest in the world, is gone? Who will take charge? Will other chipmakers take advantage of the chaos to surpass the Geforce maker? Will Jensen be the one to put a pin to the AI bubble? Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, systems editor Tobias Mann, and reporter Dan Robinson to talk about the Jensen Huang affair(s) and how the misdeeds of one of AI's biggest names could reshape the entire industry on this week's episode. A lightly edited transcript is included below:

Hey everyone and welcome to another episode of The Register’s Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg Reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and the big news on the tech industry's mind this week is the ouster of Nvidia founder, CEO, president, and board member Jensen Huang over allegations that he not only had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, but also at least two Nvidia employees who were his subordinates.

Nvidia's been shaped into one of the most valuable companies in the world over the past thirty-three years, and Huang has played a pivotal, if not the pivotal, role in that ascension, meaning his controversial departure is going to rock the industry, if not the greater world. With me to discuss this is our systems editor Tobias Mann and Reg reporter Dan Robinson. Thanks to you both for coming on.

Quite the week, huh? It seems like we went from Jensen’s just going to survive this spy kerfuffle to the board basically seeming to demand his resignation in the course of a few days, right? So Dan, bring us up to speed on the timeline here, what happened?

Well, it all happened over the last couple of weeks. That was when the story first surfaced, or it was first reported in the media, of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who happened to work for this company in Singapore that bought a lot of Nvidia's products.

Right, company was Megaspeed, right? And her name's Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, coincidence.

So it's all happened fairly quickly, but like you say, at the start of this week, it all seemed like Jensen could weather the storm. We were discussing this in our editorial chat and we thought that basically there isn't really anybody who could replace him, or so we thought. He practically is Nvidia, and it's been his vision that's driven the company for so long. But then he came out and he confessed and said he was sorry to all the Nvidia employees. Then the second affair came to light and very quickly, on November 11th actually, Wednesday, he handed in his resignation and it was accepted by the board. So we got to hear about it yesterday [Thursday] when they announced it and it was filed with the SEC.

And since then a third affair has come out, right? The New York Times published a finding.

It seems so. Makes you wonder how many others may be about to come out in the following days.

We're not going to speculate, but my gosh, it seems like that leather jacket really made him irresistible. It’s kind of crazy, right? It seems like the internal affairs with Nvidia employees are the ones that sort of broke the board's back, right? The spy affair seemed like it was kind of like…. Apparently American authorities have basically said they've found no direct evidence to say she is a spy.

It could just be that she runs a chip company too, or at least a company that is dealing in servers and datacenters. So she has a business reason beyond politics to potentially want to get involved with Jensen. What do you guys think? Was it the internal elements that finally kind of broke the camel's back here and forced the board to act?

I think that was the final straw. I think quite possibly he could have weathered the storm as we were saying, if it had just been the one affair outside the business.

Outside the business, right? Because now like you were saying, Tobias, not only do you have potentially an international spy affair, but you also have an HR issue to contend with.

Right. And I do think that the board could wave their hands around an alleged honeypot scenario. “He was targeted, this was a deliberate act, they preyed on his insecurity.”

“It wasn't as big as it's made out to be in the media.”

They could make up any number of excuses that they wanted in order to wave their hands over it and keep him CEO or if their arms were twisted by US intelligence services they could have taken him out of an executive role and pushed him into a chairmanship. They had options.

And then you had the HR kerfuffle of him allegedly sleeping with another employee. And at that point now there's a pattern. I do sort of question once the news came out that he had an extramarital affair with an employee, whether or not that had influenced him being targeted by Megaspeed and or the Chinese intelligence service, assuming those allegations prove out.

We don't know the timeline on one or the other, do we?

Right, no. And so it could be that the Chinese intelligence service became aware that this was an avenue that could be exploited and they took it. It's not lost on anybody that he spent most of the last year and a half lobbying to get his chips back into China. And largely successfully on the US side of things. It's been held up by Beijing, which kind of undermines that theory a little bit.

It seems like if she was a spy doing China's bidding and he managed to get the Trump administration to allow those older chips in, then Beijing wouldn't have been like, “No, screw you, we're making our own….”

But there's the other allegation here, which was that Alice Huang and Megaspeed were smuggling GPUs. Their operation in Singapore was set up such to bring more modern GPUs into the market. And so it could have been that Beijing  all of this is alleged  didn't really care for its model labs getting old hardware. So they could appear to be blocking us and promoting their own chips while smuggling in more advanced silicon from Nvidia through Singapore.

Through Alice Huang's company, essentially, right? So I know Jensen's going to be appearing before Congress to talk about all this, right? This is not over by a long shot, right?

So, I don't think that we should play up the gray market and the black market side of the GPU smuggling operation too much. I highly doubt Jensen knew anything about that, other than he was aware that it happens. But gray market and black market smuggling, as anybody who's worked in the electronics and the technology field will know is nothing new.

When I was a young kid in college, gray market cameras, if you needed a new camera, was a great way to save a couple hundred bucks on a camera so long as you weren't expecting a warranty to come with it. So I wouldn't read too much into the smuggling side of things. I think that's happening, but I don't think Jensen's involved at all.

It's hard to ignore the fact that he spent the last year and a half lobbying Washington to allow chips into China, more powerful chips into China. And even prior to that, he had instructed his engineers to develop China-specific accelerators and cut down owned fuse off cores, whatever it took in order to limbo under export controls. And it was not particularly popular with the last administration. Gina Raimondo openly criticized Nvidia about how they were taking the spirit of the law out of context and Nvidia pushed back a little bit about that.

That's right. She did say at one point that whatever Nvidia did to get around the rules, they were going to change them to block him.

And she eventually walked that back a little bit, because the rules are there, and so you can't really get too upset with somebody for trying to abide by the rules. Was Nvidia following the spirit of it? No.

Sure. That's a huge potential market for Nvidia, right? China is a massive market and they have a huge appetite for chips, right?

In one quarter They wrote off ten and a half billion dollars of potential profits because they could not ship H20s to China because the Trump administration kneejerked.

I remember when that story came out. That was a huge amount of money, right? How much of their market is Singapore in that area? It's some massive chunk of change.

And Dan, you probably are aware of this as well. So there's a lot of companies that operate out of Singapore but don't actually have data centers there because it's not a particularly power-dense area for them. And so there's a lot of companies that, if you look at it at face value, looks like they're importing a lot of GPUs to Singapore, but the GPUs don't dor the most part don't actually make it there.

I think Simon [Sharwood] wrote a piece recently, I think it was actually just yesterday, where he mentioned that in one case, Singaporean buyers sometimes account for over twenty percent of the quarterly revenue for Nvidia. So that's a huge market, right? Whether or not those chips are ending up in Singapore or China or some other country that's operating as a territorial expansion of Singapore for serving data centers to them, that's a lot of money. And that market could grow immensely. So, there's a fair argument to be made there that in Jensen's just being a capitalist, right? He sees a market opportunity. He's going to try to take it, it's not a conspiracy. It's not necessarily that the company's acting in collusion with China to circumvent imports. It's just, well, we got this opportunity, so we're going to follow the letter of the law, not the spirit. I don't think it's necessarily fair to fault Nvidia for that.

And Simon wrote [the] story which was about the Singaporean authorities saying that they were having a very hard time getting cooperation from the US authorities when they were investigating Megaspeed. So it does make you wonder if this really is a spying thing or if they're really worried about the smuggling, why were they not cooperating with the Singaporean authorities over this?

There's something else going on there, isn't there?

Very possibly. So OK, so more broadly, stepping back from just Nvidia and its trials and tribulations as one of the world's most largely successful companies, Tobias, you watch the chip industry. It's your thing here at the Reg. And watching chips obviously nowadays means watching Nvidia. I'm sure this is going to have an impact on the AI industry, the tech industry. And possibly beyond, right? So what have you been hearing from people you talk to, from other companies, from Nvidia itself, that is going to point to how this is going to impact the space?

I just saw this morning, I think it was Wired had a piece out, that there's some disbelief and some upset within Nvidia's own employees right now. Bring the boss back.

I think some are petitioning to bring him back.

And I think one of the things that can't be overstated is there's no real replacement for Jensen. He is the face of the company and they're now in the middle of an identity crisis. Ian Buck, who runs their HPC division and is the father of CUDA, is favored by many as a possible replacement. But I don't know that that's something Ian really wants to do. And while he's taken a much more public role in the last couple years, I don't know that he has the pull and the same degree of charisma that Jensen did in order to kind of reshape reality. The joke used to be that Steve Jobs had a reality distortion field. And that was certainly true of Jensen. Right now, Colette Kress, the acting CEO, who is the bean counter keeping Nvidia's operations and Jensen's ambitions grounded for the last 13 years, is acting CEO but I don't think she's going to be long term in that position.

Sure. It's interesting you say like keeping Jensen's ambitions grounded, right? But I know a lot of people have been talking about how a large part of the reason that Nvidia turned into what it is is because of Jensen Huang's bets that he's made over the years. Betting that GPU architecture was going to be a good model for AI was one of the reasons the company exploded to the way it is. So I wonder if she could go on to keeping Nvidia on pace, right? Because she doesn't maybe have the risk-taking nature that Jensen did or does.

Right. So this is the give and take of that relationship as far as I've seen it over the years. Things didn't always go well for Nvidia. There was a lot of hard pivots that they had to do in order to keep the business growing. You may recall back to when the pandemic shut down the economy. There was a hard pivot to selling GPUs for crypto mining because at least that's where the money was coming from. And while it was not at all popular with PC enthusiasts, it did keep revenues coming in. And so there were certainly risks and rewards that were measured. And I have no doubt that Kress was heavily involved in that. With that said, I don't think that she is the personality, how to say this, caricature. I don't think that she is the person to replace Huang unless the culture is going to change dramatically.

You can't imagine a CFO having this sort of vision thing that Jensen Huang has had to push all these various projects and everything that he does on stage with the dancing robots and what have you.

And Jensen was an engineer, right? The company was headed by an engineer for 33 years. That creates a certain culture, right? You don't want this to turn to another Boeing situation, right? Where the bean counters take over and the company suddenly becomes so risk averse that they're just doing anything they can to keep the profits coming in, which leads to an inferior product.

And to draw some comparisons, this is not the first time we've seen something like that happen. Bob Swan's tenure at Intel as CEO, he was forced out because he could not take, he was running it like a CFO. He had been the CFO. He was forced out and replaced by Gelsinger, whose unchecked ambition proved too much for the board in the end. So there is some grounding that is required in companies this large in order to keep personality and ambition from getting in the way of the business, and vice versa. In this chaos, however, there's great opportunity for other players right now. And it's not going to be the clean fight, I don't think, that any of us would necessarily want to see.

Any ideas who comes out on top or too early to tell?

You can't ignore the fact that Nvidia is still the biggest player in this space and that's going to remain true. The execution over the roadmap, the existing roadmap, is going to tell us whether or not the company is going to survive long term. Having said that, from a technological standpoint, hardware is not Nvidia's advantage right now.

AMD has caught up and in some ways surpassed Nvidia in terms of accelerators and chips. So Lisa Su is in a great position to capitalize on this right now. There is an emerging push from hyperscalers and increasingly model devs towards semi-custom hardware developed in collaboration with companies like Broadcom and Marvell. And so if...in this chaos, hyperscalers go, I'm going to insulate myself from the potential that the roadmap may fall apart by investing more in our in-house silicon, you could see Nvidia's claim over the market decline over this time. And at the same time, you could also see chip startups asking inconvenient questions about how far does the rot go? Can Nvidia's chips be trusted? And it's not like chipmakers haven't been calling that into question for years now. Three years ago, Cerebras's CEO called out Jensen as un-American and an AI arms dealer for insisting on selling chips to China. I fully expect there's going to be quite a bit of underhanded dealing and playing off of all of this conspiracy going forward.

Like I was saying earlier, it was there before, those claims of Nvidia being a risk or there being conspiracies surrounding their Chinese market. I can't imagine that slows down now.

That said, there are an awful lot of firearms manufacturers accused of being arms dealers during prior wars that are still kicking, so…

Absolutely. Absolutely. I guess the continued success of any of these companies again sort of hinges on whether frontier models continue to be the de facto norm in AI computing, right? Because that could change as well.

There's a lot of things that could happen. The reality is the bubble is here because there is a disconnect between the actual value of these goods and services and the prescribed value of these goods and services. If that gets brought back to reality, the bubble pops. If it happens quickly, it's going to be tremendously damaging to economies. If it happens slowly, things could play out much cleaner. But, there's a lot of people who are concerned right now that Huang may be the one that pops the bubble.

Pops the bubble. That's what I was going to ask next was basically, is this a bubble-popping moment for AI? Does Jensen's ouster, is Jensen's ouster the pin that pops this bubble? Do either of you have any thoughts then?

I'm going to let Dan answer that question first.

Well, people have been asking questions about Nvidia's financing of a lot of the AI industry.

They're kind of key to a lot of the circular investing that's been going on.

So you do start to wonder how many of these AI companies, especially like the rent-a-GPU cloud companies, how many of those are being kept going by investment from Nvidia and whether that's going to continue with the CFO in charge. And also whoever happens to be the follow-on chief executive, will they continue to do that kind of thing? If so, maybe that could start to let some of the air out of the AI bubble.

Those neoclouds are always kind of the ones that are canaries in the coal mine, so to speak, in this industry.

That's what we think. I would agree with what Dan had to add there. I would note there's two elements that I'm sort of watching. Whoever ends up being the new CEO is going to have an awful lot of say in terms of how additional funding and investment takes place. Nvidia invests in neoclouds in two ways. One of them is direct funding. They'll invest money and it's tied to a procurement agreement. So if they're going to use that money to buy our chips, we're going to help facilitate that. The other side of it is that GPUs are so valuable and in such demand. It's particularly Nvidia's GPUs, which are seen by the market as being the most valuable and most potent, which isn't necessarily true as I mentioned earlier. If that valuation of the prescribed value of those GPUs declined, getting debt backed by those GPUs, kind of like collateral on an auto loan, might get much, much more difficult because the reason that neoclouds are able to go get billions of dollars in loans is because the lenders believe that the assets are still going to be worth something if the company isn't successful.

And llke you said, there could just be a first domino to get pushed. What do you guys think about the potential of Tim Cook being Jensen's replacement as Donald Trump has suggested. Tim Apple.

My bet would be on Jensen making a surprise return before Tim.

I don't think that Tim Cook wants to take over at Nvidia.

Well not just that, but Tim's success was driven in large part by driving a logistics monster at Apple, ensuring that they always had the materials that they needed and anticipating market changes before they happened so that things like when the memory crisis hit, Apple's prices were insulated for several months and they could gain sales because people wouldn't buy others' products because they were getting more expensive faster. I don't think that that is something that Nvidia needs right now.

That's totally fair. Also I feel like Tim Cook is a bit I mean, we've called him bland on several occasions and I feel like the risk-taking nature may not be there in the same way that Jensen's kind of jet setting super hip tech man vibe gave Nvidia. I don't know. Dan, what are your thoughts?

I don't know. I don't know about Tim Cook. Like you say. I'm not going to say he's bland because that's unkind.

You're more diplomatic than we are, I guess.

About some of the other names that have been put forward by people taking odds on this have been Lisa Su. But I couldn't see her leaving AMD really.

Tobias shaking his head over here, yeah. No.

Or Rene Haas from Arm. Who does share a lot of the same views on things as Jensen Huang did, especially on AI and on the physical AI on robots being the next big thing. So. I don't know, that could position him as a potential candidate. Who knows, would you want to step into the potential mess that's been left by Jensen's departure?

I think it's pretty telling that most of the candidates outside of Nvidia are already the CEO of major technology companies. There's like Lip-Bu Tan at Intel, I could see, if he wasn't already at Intel, making that jump. And maybe he will. Intel is still kind of a mess. But it is somewhat telling that there's just not many good candidates to fill that role that aren't already in that position.

Jensen Huang is, I feel like it's akin to Apple hunting for a successor to Steve Jobs, right? Apple was Steve Jobs for many years, in the same way that Jensen lived 33 years at the helm of this company, from it being a tiny startup to being the behemoth that it is now. I don't want to call it a cult of personality, but Jensen Huang, like you said before, was in many ways Nvidia. This is a huge shift for this company, especially with the amount of influence that it has. So any thoughts on what might be next for Jensen? Does he come out with a new startup? Is this an OpenAI sort of thing where the storm ebbs and he returns? Any thoughts?

That's difficult to say. He might go for a startup. According to the company's proxy statement that was filed some time ago, he could be in for a $264 million payout for his termination which... He may just want to go to Hawaii and retire.

Maybe, I know Tobias, I think you mentioned in your story that you don't think that this is the end of his career in the space. He's just got too much get up and go and too much ambition to just walk away.

There's the ambition and the cult of personality. So I would imagine he's probably going to disappear from the spotlight for a little while. Might be months, it might be a couple years. Without knowing the terms of his contract and his mobility in terms of being able to stand up a competing startup. Assuming that's what he even wants to do. But his cult of personality is such that, if he did start a new company, there would be very little stopping folks from jumping ship very quickly from Nvidia to come work for him. They may have to go take a two-year hiatus, but right now would not be the worst time to cash out some Nvidia stock to take a break for two years and go back to work for the old boss either.

He might be on dangerous territory if he tried to go into a startup making AI accelerators though.

Who knows? Maybe he will trade spaces with Lip-Bu and go run Intel.

Just a good old shuffling of leadership here.

He was actually joking with the press and analysts at GTC that Intel has had 10 CEOs in the last 30 years and Nvidia has only had one. Famous last words, I guess.

Well, we'll see. It's going to be an interesting few weeks to kind of watch this unfold. I know he's testifying before Congress soon on the whole matter. The investigations into the Alice Huang matter aren't done. And I'm sure there's more revelations and shakeups to come in Nvidia. And we will be right here to write about it at the register and talk about it on The Kettle. Thanks for joining us and we will talk to you soon. ®

#10110. Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new form factor that lets you run standard HTTP web applications on Lambda without rewriting your code into an event handler. You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.

With this launch, AWS Lambda now offers three distinct form factors, each built on the same Firecracker isolation technology and designed for a different programming model.

Lambda Event Functions are what you already know as Lambda functions. They use the event-driven, single-concurrent handler model with wall-clock billing. We’re introducing the “Event Functions” name to highlight that programming model: your function receives an event, processes it, and returns a response. The event-driven programming model is ideal for event processing, queue consumers, and invocations triggered by other AWS services.

Lambda Web Functions use an HTTP-native programming model with multi-concurrent execution and active CPU billing. Your code listens on a port and handles standard HTTP requests. That programming model is ideal for web applications, API backends, and interactive HTTP workloads where multiple concurrent requests and I/O-heavy processing are the norm.

Lambda MicroVMs provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments with customer-managed lifecycles for running untrusted or user-generated code.

The three complement each other. An application might use Event Functions for asynchronous backend processing, Web Functions for the user-facing API and server-side rendering layer, and MicroVMs for interactive code execution features, all within the same AWS account and sharing the same operational model.

Why Web FunctionsModern web applications need to serve global audiences with fast, consistent response times while giving developers the freedom to use standard frameworks and iterate quickly. Building this today typically requires assembling multiple infrastructure components, configuring multi-region deployments, setting up latency-based routing, and tuning billing models to avoid paying for I/O wait. Developers often find themselves adapting their application code to fit a specific compute model rather than deploying the HTTP server they already have.

Lambda Web Functions removes this complexity. Each execution environment handles multiple requests simultaneously (up to 128 concurrent requests per environment), which means a burst of incoming traffic can share warm environments instead of mapping each request to a new one. Web Functions meter the CPU time your code uses, so time spent waiting on a database query or an API call consumes little CPU. Memory is metered for as long as the execution environment exists. For I/O-heavy web workloads like server-side rendering, API backends, and AI inference endpoints streaming token responses, this can reduce compute costs.

Let’s try it outTo get started, I wrote a simple Express.js server. This is the same code I run locally with node index.js, no Lambda-specific adapters or wrappers required.

The only difference from running locally is the AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT environment variable, which Lambda sets to the host and port your server must listen on. To run locally, set it yourself, for example AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:3000 node index.js.

With my code ready, I deployed using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI):

One command. No prior resource setup. The CLI bundled my source, created the Web Function, published its first revision, attached a Web Function endpoint, and returned a live HTTPS URL in under a minute.

A revision is an immutable snapshot of the code I deployed. The endpoint is the HTTPS URL that routes traffic to a revision, or splits traffic across revisions. Those are the resources I use to iterate and to control how traffic moves to new code.

Next, I wanted my application to serve users in Europe and Asia with lower latency. I redeployed with multiple regions:

Lambda Web Functions replicated my code to all three regions and configured latency-based routing automatically. Each request now routes to the Region with the lowest latency for the caller, on a best-effort basis, through one global URL (.lambda-web.global.on.aws).

When I updated my code and ran the same deploy command again, the CLI detected the existing function, uploaded the new revision, and pointed the endpoint at it. Total turnaround from code change to live: seconds.

For production workflows that require a more gradual rollout, I can shift traffic between revisions with a single API call:

This sends 90% of endpoint traffic to the current revision and 10% to the new one, giving me a canary deployment without additional tooling.

Better together with Amazon CloudFrontFor applications that combine static and dynamic content, Web Functions works well alongside Amazon CloudFront. You can select a Web Function endpoint as the origin for your CloudFront distribution. Static assets are served from the cache while dynamic requests route to your Web Function, giving you CDN performance for static content with serverless compute for the dynamic parts.

Web Functions improves the private-origin experience with CloudFront. With this launch, you attach CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to a Web Function endpoint instead. CloudFront signs requests to the origin, and the endpoint allows only your distribution to invoke it. You get the same private-origin pattern CloudFront already provides for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), without exposing the endpoint or adding custom authorization to your app.

Now availableAWS Lambda Web Functions is available today in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). Web Functions run Node.js 24 (nodejs24.x) on Arm64 at launch and support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.

To get started, deploy your first Web Function in under a minute:

For pricing details, visit the AWS Lambda pricing page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions documentation.

Micah Walter is a Sr. Solutions Architect supporting enterprise customers in the New York City region and beyond. He advises executives, engineers, and architects at every step along their journey to the cloud, with a deep focus on sustainability and practical design. In his free time, Micah enjoys the outdoors, photography, and chasing his kids around the house.

#10108. Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric

Appliances can share 16 TB of DRAM and half a terabyte of HBM across up to 16 systems

Celestial AI’s dream of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) at a distance will soon be a reality as part of a new collaboration between Marvell Technology and system integrator Penguin Solutions to build a photonic memory fabric.

Marvell acquired the underlying technology for the fabric from Celestial AI for $3.5 billion in February. It comprises a memory expansion module with two stacks of HBM3e totaling 72 GB along with support for eight channels of DDR5 stacked atop a silicon photonic interposer with 7.2 Tbps (900 GB/s) of bidirectional bandwidth.

“What we provide in this appliance is what we call a Photonic Fabric memory module… We provide these modules to Penguin, and they build the box, do all the power management, do the software, and all the management layer,” Preet Virk, senior VP of Marvell’s photonic fabric biz, tells El Reg.

Penguin’s first appliances based on the tech will support 16 of these memory modules for up to 16 TB of DDR5 and 1 TB of HBM, with future systems capable of scaling to twice the DDR5 capacity.

With 57.6 Tbps of bandwidth distributed via a Marvell-designed optical fiber shuffle, each appliance supports up to 16 servers either via a network interface card, or via co-packaged (CPO) or near-packaged optical (NPO) modules.

If you’re not familiar, CPO modules are typically integrated directly into the compute or switch ASIC, while NPO modules are a sort of half measure. They connect electrically to the host, whether that’s a CPU, GPU, or some other ASIC, and the rest of the fabric optically. NPO is expected to play a major role in the next generation of rack-scale systems from Nvidia and AMD, as it provides better serviceability and lower blast radius than baking photonic chiplets directly into CPUs or GPUs.

Through a software layer, which we’re told was developed by Penguin, each system can access the entire shared memory space, similar to how systems connecting to network-attached storage would have access to the appliance's full capacity.

As we understand it, a lot of this functionality is made possible today through CXL 3.1 compatible NICs and host CPUs, like AMD’s shiny new Venice CPUs. However, for NPO- and CPO-based memory, Virk tells us that CXL can be bypassed entirely.

Amid the AI-fueled memory crunch, will Compute Express Link finally have its moment to shine?

The implications of this tech should be obvious. If memory can be shared and pooled across multiple servers, each of those servers doesn't need as much of its own DRAM, possibly saving some money.

In addition to facilitating communications, Virk says, the software also allows for several memory tiering modes by which customers can expose the resources to connected systems. For the most part, these follow typical CXL memory tiering conventions, with the exception of an HBM cache-through mode that Virk says will enable users to extract the performance of HBM with the capacity of DDR5.

This mode essentially treats the HBM as a read/write cache. Frequently accessed files are written to and read from HBM first before being pushed into standard DDR5 as they get stale.

Marvell and Penguin are positioning the new memory appliance as an alternative to storage-based key value (KV) cache offload. AI inference generates large KV caches, which are used to track model state across chat sessions, and long-running agents. Depending on the context length, these caches can be both computationally expensive to recompute and large to keep in memory.

Because of this, inactive KV caches are often offloaded to DRAM or flash memory, since it’s faster to store and copy them than to recompute them if and when a session is restored. Marvell contends that by offloading KV caches from HBM directly to these memory appliances, customers can achieve better performance and higher memory utilization.

Beyond AI-adjacent workloads, this technology also has potential to reduce the amount of DRAM required for individual systems, a concept we explored in greater depth earlier this year, and one that Meta has already embraced in its own datacenters.

Marvell expects Penguin’s first generation of Photonic Fabric memory expansion systems to arrive sometime in the second half of next year. ®

#10105. AWS Weekly Roundup: Prime Day 2026 by the numbers, Claude Haiku 5.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, and more (October 13, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment. Last week we published the Prime Day 2026 metrics, and the one that stuck with me is 2.3 quadrillion: the daily requests Amazon ElastiCache peaked at during the event. Prime Day ran back in June, so this post always lands as a retrospective, and that gap is part of what makes it worth reading. By the time the numbers reach you, the only evidence that any of it happened is that nothing went wrong.

The rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained. Claude Haiku 5.5 arrived on Amazon Bedrock at roughly 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic made voice agents quicker on their feet, and Strands Box showed up to put real boundaries around what an agent is allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesAll the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head. Over the four days of Prime Day, Amazon DynamoDB processed more than 59 trillion requests while peaking at 192 million requests per second, and kept single-digit millisecond responses throughout. AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day. Amazon EBS peaked above 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving more than an exabyte of data daily. Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, a 47.7 percent jump over last year, and AWS Graviton powered up to 49 percent of the Amazon EC2 compute that Amazon.com used.

The number I keep coming back to, though, isn’t a throughput record. The team ran more than 44,000 AWS Fault Injection Service experiments ahead of the event, more than six times what they ran in 2025. Those are deliberate failures injected on purpose, months in advance, so that the trillions of requests above turn into an ordinary shopping afternoon. If you’re preparing for your own peak moment, AWS Countdown Premium is built for exactly that kind of planning.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#10104. Google: AI agent turned a security patch into a working exploit with no human help

A suspected Russian-speaking operator used an AI agent to turn security patches into working exploits with no human in the loop – a first such occurrence, according to the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) – before ultimately stealing data from victim organizations.

Google documented this attack in its fourth-quarter 2026 AI threat tracker, and said it marks a significant advance in how attackers use LLMs for fully autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation compared to Q3.

In this case, the threat hunters found an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with multiple frontier and local models. The framework, called exploit_agent, used Russian-language tooling, and was configured to conduct continuous differential analysis of “popular web application software,” according to the report.

This includes comparing code before and after security updates, identifying potential vulnerabilities, developing exploits, and then automatically executing them without any human involvement.

The server also contained data stolen from victim organizations, and “multiple” post-compromise scripts that allowed attackers to perform nefarious activities including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells.

“Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector,” according to the report.

The report also documents other instances of attackers moving beyond manual LLM prompting during cyberattacks and instead deploying autonomous, multi-agent offensive security frameworks to carry out multi-stage intrusions. These include both financially motivated cybercriminals and cyber-espionage groups.

In addition to the recent attacks involving the open source penetration-testing tool ARTEX, attackers have also used other AI-powered offensive frameworks, including CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike AI, and PentAGI. In another instance, GTIG observed attackers using PentAGI alongside proxy services to target the aerospace sector.

“We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus,” the Googlers wrote. “Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally.” ®

#10101. Amazon S3 is now available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow. Starting today, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), including Amazon S3 Tables and Amazon S3 Vectors, is natively available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel, covering three distinct workloads: everyday storage, analytics, and AI.

Why this matters Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel. Storage is essential to performant applications, but provisioning it previously required navigating to the AWS Management Console to configure policies and credentials. Now, S3 storage integrates directly into the Vercel developer experience, with resource provisioning and connection configuration handled automatically. Together with existing integrations for Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, you get a complete application stack inside Vercel (from your database layer through to object, vector, and open table storage), all on one AWS account with one bill.

Figure 1 – The AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

Getting started From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create. Select AWS, pick your S3 bucket type, choose a Region, and create the bucket. Provisioning takes a few seconds.

Figure 2 – Creating an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket in Vercel by choosing a Region and a name.

Connect the bucket to a project, then pull the environment variables with the Vercel CLI:

The integration injects AWS_REGION, AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_RESOURCE_ARN, and a bucket name such as S3_BUCKET_NAME, S3_TABLE_BUCKET_NAME, or S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME. At runtime, the awsCredentialsProvider from @vercel/functions/oidc exchanges a short-lived OIDC token with AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) for temporary credentials scoped to your resource. No static keys are stored anywhere.

Object storage with S3 This Next.js route uploads a file to a general purpose bucket:

Use ListObjectsV2Command and GetObjectCommand with the same client to list and read objects.

Analytics with S3 Tables S3 Tables offer S3 storage purpose-built for analytics and are designed to automatically optimize query performance as data volumes grow. They provide fully managed Apache Iceberg tables with automated table maintenance and compaction, and they work with any Apache Iceberg REST Catalog-compliant engine. You can use DuckDB inside a Vercel Function for lightweight queries. This example attaches the table bucket by its ARN and runs an aggregate query:

If you run DuckDB inside a Next.js route, add @duckdb/node-api to serverExternalPackages in next.config.mjs so the native bindings are not bundled.

Vector search with S3 Vectors S3 Vectors deliver purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage for AI agents, AI inference, and semantic search of your content stored in Amazon S3. S3 Vectors provides native support for storing and querying vectors without a separate vector database, but it does not generate them. Create the embeddings with your model of choice, then query the index for the closest matches:

Building with v0 by Vercel From v0, describe what you want to build and it provisions the right resource. Ask for “a photo gallery where users upload images using AWS” to get a general purpose bucket, “a support bot that answers questions from my PDFs” to get S3 Vectors, or “an analytics dashboard for my clickstream data” to get S3 Tables. v0 then configures the connection and generates working code.

Figure 3 – v0 generating a PDF support bot from a natural language prompt, with Amazon S3 Vectors connected and the application in the Preview panel.

Combining S3 with AWS databases Every AWS service on Vercel shares the same account and authentication model, so you can combine them with no extra setup. For example, store file metadata in Aurora with the files in S3, or store document text in DynamoDB with embeddings in S3 Vectors for RAG retrieval.

Using Vercel with your AWS account You can create a new AWS account through the integration, which supports S3 features for building and testing. You can also link an existing AWS account to use your full set of S3 and AWS capabilities and keep your current billing. If you link an existing AWS account, Vercel works only with new buckets that you create through the platform. Because every S3 resource lives in your own AWS account, you keep AWS-native tooling and a single place to manage storage.

Pricing and availability There is no charge for the integration, and you pay standard Amazon S3 pricing for the resources you use. New AWS accounts created through Vercel receive $100 in credits valid for six months. Amazon S3, including S3 Tables and S3 Vectors, is available from v0 and the Vercel Marketplace in all commercial AWS Regions supported by Vercel. To get started, visit v0 or the AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

Join the conversation If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. Share your feedback on AWS re:Post for Amazon S3.

#10099. Microsoft Outlook outage blamed after 15 injured in hotel pool chlorine incident

A safety warning went missing, chemical levels soared, and five guests ended up in hospital

Most victims of last week's Microsoft outage lost access to their email, but 15 unlucky guests at a German hotel got a dose of chlorine when a warning about dangerous levels never reached staff.

The incident, first reported by German broadcaster WDR, happened on Friday at Hotel Ling Bao, part of the Phantasialand theme park in Brühl, Germany, where a malfunctioning automatic dosing system pumped too much chlorine into the swimming pool.

The hotel's monitoring system spotted the problem and emailed staff a warning about the excessive chlorine levels. Unfortunately, Microsoft's Outlook service was caught up in a global outage, meaning the warning never arrived.

Brühl Fire Department said the problem started when a technical fault caused the pool's dosing equipment to pump in more chlorine than it should have. Chlorine gas then escaped into the swimming area, leaving guests needing medical attention.

Paramedics checked over 15 people at the hotel, and five were taken to hospital. Four suffered minor injuries, while one was moderately injured and needed further treatment. The fire department sent about 40 personnel to the scene, and crews spent roughly two hours dealing with the incident.

The incident came as Microsoft was battling a major outage that began on Thursday, November 12, and dragged well into Friday. Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and other Microsoft 365 services were knocked offline, leaving businesses unable to access email and documents. The disruption wasn't confined to office workers unable to check their inboxes, with hospitals, police forces, and government departments reporting problems accessing the Microsoft services they use for day-to-day operations.

Redmond has since blamed the outage on a bug introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade. It sat there until a later network change set it off, and the failures then spread across the company's infrastructure. Microsoft ruled out both cybercriminals and AI as culprits, and has issued the customary apology.

At Phantasialand, though, a broken inbox was the least of anyone's worries.

The chlorine dosing equipment went haywire independently of Microsoft's troubles, but the email warning staff about the problem apparently never arrived. Whether the hotel had a backup alarm, or anything capable of shutting off the chlorine supply automatically, remains unanswered.

Why a hotel would rely on Outlook to deliver warnings about dangerous chlorine levels is anyone's guess. Email can be delayed, filtered into spam, or simply disappear when Microsoft's infrastructure throws a tantrum, none of which is particularly helpful when you've got a pool with guests breathing in noxious gas. ®

#10097. AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Lambda Web Functions, Amazon S3 on the Vercel Marketplace, and more (October 19, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Nothing last week added a new kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. AWS Lambda learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and Amazon S3 became something you can provision from inside the tool you were already using, without opening the AWS Management Console. Different services, same direction.

The counterweight arrived on Thursday. As it gets easier to put things into production, it matters more that you can say what those things are allowed to do, and this week’s most interesting read is about exactly that. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesAWS Lambda Web Functions is a new form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler. You take a port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, or Next.js, run aws lambda-web deploy, and get back a live HTTPS URL in under a minute. No adapters, no infrastructure to set up first, no framework lock-in. Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation, which compose inside one application: Event Functions (the model you already know) for async work, Web Functions for the user-facing layer, and MicroVMs for stateful sandboxes running untrusted code.

Two details make this more than repackaging. Each execution environment handles up to 128 concurrent requests, so a burst of traffic shares warm environments instead of mapping one request to one environment, and billing meters the CPU time your code actually uses rather than wall-clock time. For server-side rendering, API backends, and inference endpoints streaming tokens, where most of the elapsed time is spent waiting, that changes the arithmetic. Adding --regions to the same deploy command replicates your code and configures latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and you can split traffic across revisions by weight for a canary rollout. It’s available in five Regions, running Node.js 24 on Arm64 with VPC connectivity. The AWS Compute Blog has a longer walkthrough, and Amazon CloudFront can now use a Web Function endpoint as an origin with origin access control.

The week’s other headline isn’t a launch. Trust in Depth: giving agents more autonomy without losing control makes an argument I keep running into in practice: putting a person in the loop for every agent action works at small scale and then quietly stops working, because people asked to check everything stop catching what matters. The alternative is four questions answered at four moments, which AWS calls scope, know, bound, and observe. The part worth sitting with is that an agent’s limits belong outside its own reasoning, in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policies enforced at the gateway, because an agent cannot turn off a control it does not run. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, including AWS Identity and Access Management at more than 2.1 billion requests per second, and the case here is for pointing it at the rules you write for agents.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

#10095. How Young People Are Researching Issues That Matter to Them

“Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student Middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code. They engaged in research to explore how administrators, teachers, and staff could incorporate their voices in decision-making processes. Students conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers and developed recommendations for their school, including more student-led events and a more active role engaged in school policy discussions. The following semester, the principal added students to several school leadership committees, where they helped inform programs and policies beyond the dress code, such as student social events and classroom curricular activities. Many youth across the U.S. report feeling disengaged and disconnected from their schools, which is associated with declining attendance and greater mental health challenges. Addressing these challenges is critical, especially because a sense of belonging and connectedness predicts attendance, academic success, social well-being, self-esteem, and other positive outcomes for students. Research is one important way to seek out solutions to these problems, and Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) is an innovative and growing approach that engages youth as experts to improve their lives, communities, and youth-serving institutions. In middle and high schools across the U.S., students in YPAR classes conduct research to inform policies, practices, and peer education efforts. They have prioritized and addressed a wide range of academic and school-climate issues, such as improving teacher-student relationships, peer relationships, safety, and school lunch options; and reducing disproportionate discipline, substance use, and transit barriers. In schools that provide opportunities for YPAR, students are trained to take up roles as researchers, knowledge producers, and changemakers who contribute to their school communities. Further, YPAR evidence can deepen adults’ understanding of what shapes students’ feelings of belonging, patterns of engagement, and well-being. YPAR findings thus can inform more relevant and responsive solutions that can benefit youth, adults, and the broader community. This article provides guidance for educators who work with K–12 students and are interested in implementing YPAR. The impacts of YPAR in K–12 schools Here are three examples of how YPAR impacts different levels of the school “ecosystem.” Systems-level: High school YPAR students in an Ohio school district explored whether their school provided adequate mental health services. They conducted a schoolwide survey, and their findings revealed that although there were mental health services available, many students were not aware of them. In response, the student researchers took action and developed more promotional materials and held informational assemblies to raise awareness of these services. They also held meetings with teachers, counselors, administrators, and the superintendent to discuss potential districtwide solutions to improve mental health services and access. Relationships: Middle school YPAR students in a California school district identified that they didn’t feel supported by their teachers. To explore this issue further, they conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers on teacher-student relationships. Their findings offered concrete suggestions on how teachers could improve their mentorship relationships with students, including practicing active listening, showing respect and compassion, being more flexible with assignments, and incorporating more engaging classroom activities that lift up student voices. The students also recommended student-led teacher evaluations. Student-level: High school YPAR students in a California school district conducted English and Spanish focus groups with their peers on attendance and belonging. Based on their findings, the YPAR students proposed buddy programs to connect new students with their peers, schoolwide workshops to raise awareness on racial stereotyping, and lunchtime soccer tournaments to increase a sense of belonging. Read more stories on our YPAR Hub. Setting the stage for YPAR at your school Our YPAR Design Guide offers several considerations when deciding whether YPAR is a fit for your program or setting. YPAR has been primarily implemented with middle and high school students, and is well-suited to strengthening the developmental capacities of youth in early, middle, and late adolescence. However, elementary school students have also engaged in successful YPAR projects using mapping and arts-based methods. First, adult facilitators (for example, teachers or program leaders) should assess capacity and consider whether there are adequate resources to pursue the YPAR project, including the timeframe of the project, staffing required, whether funding is needed, and the setting and scope. Second, adult facilitators can introduce YPAR to students in a way that meets them “where they are at.” Not every student will be interested in YPAR from the start. Some may have had limited exposure to research, and others may not have had positive experiences (for example, through a particularly challenging or frustrating class assignment). Facilitators can engage the students in activities that lift up their experiences, then generate excitement by framing research as a tool for exploring and taking action on the issues that students care about. Facilitators should also work with students to clarify their motivations for the project: What is the purpose of the project? What do students hope to get out of participating in YPAR? And what does their desired impact look like? In several projects, we have seen students become more interested in YPAR as they move through the process, analyze data, and develop their action plans and recommendations. Finally, adult facilitators should be attentive to the broader context surrounding the topic or issue. For example, if the research is on safety and well-being, what programs or initiatives are already focusing on these issues, both in and out of school (for example, community health organizations)? What are the relevant constraints (for example, barriers accessing decision-making processes)? And where might there be opportunities to partner and collaborate? Understanding these factors will help adult facilitators and students choose an area of focus that aligns with their goals. What YPAR might look like YPAR is not “one size fits all.” Adult YPAR facilitators adapt YPAR across a multitude of settings, including schools, afterschool programs, and community-based organizations such as youth centers. Even within schools, a YPAR process can vary in length. For example, some YPAR projects span a single unit within a semester; others may take up an entire semester, and in some cases extend across a full academic year (fall and spring semesters). Further, YPAR is sometimes conducted as part of a club or extracurricular activity outside of formal class time. While the structure and duration of YPAR projects vary, many projects follow these steps: building the team, identifying and defining an issue or problem, selecting a research design and methods, collecting data, analyzing and interpreting results, developing action plans and recommendations, disseminating findings, and taking action. Throughout the YPAR process, young people serve as leaders who decide on the topic, issue, and questions they wish to investigate. Adult facilitators serve as supportive guides and mentors, training them in research methods focused on generating numerical data or text- and image-based data. Youth then go on to collect and analyze their data and develop actions plans and recommendations to address their selected problem. Change that starts with students A core value in YPAR is authentic power-sharing between adult facilitators and youth researchers. Most of the time, youth navigate learning spaces where they are “receivers” of knowledge from adults. Further, in traditional adult-led research projects, youth typically serve only as “respondents” to surveys or interviews, with no say in the research questions, methods, or interpretation. The YPAR approach challenges these dynamics by positioning youth as knowledge generators who combine lived-experience expertise with systematic data-based inquiry. Youth researchers have decision-making power and are primary drivers of the YPAR process, while adults serve as guides to help them in advancing their projects. Power-sharing is a learnable and teachable set of skills. Our guide provides lessons and activities that help facilitators attend to power dynamics, along with strategies that support power-sharing throughout YPAR. Adults and youth can productively share power in research when supportive structures are in place. The results from YPAR research may (or may not) result in policy or practice change. Adult facilitators play a critical role in strategically connecting YPAR evidence to key decision-making spaces and helping implement youth action plans. One step that facilitators can take is identifying existing decision-making structures where there may be opportunities to integrate YPAR evidence. They can also determine whether new routines need to be established. High School youth in Colorado investigated practices (through student surveys) that they noticed enhanced student-teacher relationships. Students then developed and led a day-long professional development for teachers on how small adjustments to the start of the year, including taking time to build trust and rapport before reviewing the syllabi, could increase student engagement and buy-in. In our work, students have consistently emphasized how much it matters for adults to “keep them in the loop,” reporting back on whether and how their YPAR evidence was used. Authentically integrating YPAR evidence involves being transparent with students and following up with them throughout the process. Adults should take YPAR evidence seriously and actively prevent tokenizing processes—in other words, where YPAR evidence becomes a check-the-box rather than meaningful engagement. Ultimately, adults supporting YPAR must take an active role in creating conditions where youth feel safe, heard, and valued. There is growing interest in YPAR at the local, state, and national levels, and it aligns with many initiatives that are already happening in schools. For example, the National Institutes of Health identified YPAR as a promising approach to address conditions that affect mental health and well-being, such as social isolation and exposure to unsafe environments. In California, SB997 mandates student voice be integrated in school and district budgeting processes. Oregon, Ohio, and New Jersey have similar mandates that require youth voice in decision making. There are strong synergies between YPAR and social-emotional learning programs, which are implemented in many school sites. YPAR also aligns with many academic competencies and standards, offering students a unique opportunity to build durable academic and career skills. Students care about their schools and want to improve them. Adults need to learn along with them, listen to them, value their ideas, and support them in making change.

#10093. Criminals attack French postal operator subsidiary, grab contact details of 22M people

France's data protection authority is looking into the intrusion after the postal service reported itself

The contact details of 22 million people were accessed after a cyberattack on a subsidiary of France's postal service, officials say.

La Poste confirmed to The Register that an attack in September had resulted in full names and postal addresses being stolen by cybercriminals.The attack targeted the systems of Maileva, a business mail platform that's part of Docaposte, the digital services arm of La Poste.

Customers use Maileva for hybrid post services. They upload the documents they need to send to Maileva, which then prints and posts the letters on behalf of the customer.

According to Maileva itself, the service has more than 70,000 registered users and is trusted to send more than 180 million documents per year.

The digital assault was first reported by French cyberattack-tracking website Cyberattaque late last week, revealing that Maileva notified customers of an attempted intrusion in late September.

The letters mentioned the cybercriminal attempting to send emails using customers' official, trusted addresses, a situation which resulted in Maileva  service disruption for six days.

A number of Maileva customers issued public statements confirming the attack in October.

Cornouaille's occupational health and safety service, for example, said the attack targeted Maileva's tracking database. It went on to say that senders' usernames and email addresses were also compromised, and that recipients' genders were exposed too, adding to the potentially affected data types that La Poste confirmed over the weekend.

Maileva told the organization it was not aware of any compromise of documents uploaded to the platform, nor did the attacker alter or destroy any data.

However, the disclosures of other customers suggested that each may have been affected differently.

In the case of the Foch hospital in Suresnes, whose debt recovery partner Kiwee was a Maileva customer, the names of documents sent to recipients may have been exposed, which may have indirectly revealed details about medical conditions.

According to Cyberattaque, the attacker also potentially accessed the contents of payment reminder letters, which in turn revealed additional details such as invoice numbers and amounts, and treatment dates.

Another case involving social housing provider Flandre Opale Habitat reportedly exposed details from letters dating back ten years.

La Poste said in a statement to The Register: "All teams are working hard to provide the best possible support to Maileva's clients and remain committed to rigorously and professionally implementing the necessary measures to ensure the security of its own operations and those of its clients."

The attack on Maileva is the second major cyber-related disruption La Poste has handled in the space of a year.

On December 22, 2025, the organization fended off a DDoS attack, which went on to affect mail operations for days, including online parcel tracking and its banking arm’s online services, right at its busiest time of the year.

La Poste described the DDoS attack as "unprecedented in its scale and power," and while it had mostly subsided by December 24, the attackers restarted it in the early hours of New Year’s Day.

The organization said the second wave comprised "several billion connection attempts per second," sent from several million IP addresses. More than 300 cybersecurity specialists were involved in defending and remediating the attack. ®

#10091. Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, update, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.

Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.

ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.

A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.

Choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.

Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.

Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.

Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.

Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:

To create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation.

ECS Gateway:Behind the scenesA gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.

Platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.

Application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.

At deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.

For each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a new one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.

ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:

Things to Know Here are a few important details to keep in mind:

Now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page.

To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Channy is a Lead Blogger of AWS News Blog and Principal Developer Advocate for AWS Cloud. As an open web enthusiast and blogger at heart, he loves community-driven learning and sharing of technology.
